transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, I guess I came in because everything sort of piled up. I’m an artist, so projects always overlap a little, and I usually like that—keeps the studio alive, you know? But lately I’ve been saying yes to too many things: workshops, client calls, fixing up the studio, new pieces I probably don’t have room to finish.

And then I was looking at the calendar—actually, it’s this huge paper one because I hate the phone calendars, they never feel real—and I realized the deadlines are all sitting on top of each other. Plus the mortgage is starting to feel like it’s breathing down my neck. So… I think I’ve taken on more than I can realistically handle, and now it’s catching up with me.
Do you find yourself feeling excessively worried or anxious about not being able to meet these deadlines or handle everything on your plate?

I don’t know if I’d call it anxious exactly. I mean, I look at the calendar and my stomach does that little drop, but then I start thinking maybe I can rearrange the whole studio wall and make a better system, because the current one is terrible—there are receipts pinned up with paint samples, it’s ridiculous.

So… worried, yes, maybe in a practical way? I’m aware there’s too much. But I don’t know if it’s “excessive” or just… I’ve made a mess of the schedule and now I’m staring at it.
Lately, have you noticed feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like your art or other activities?

I’m not sure. I mean, I still care about the art—probably too much, honestly. Sometimes I look at a half-finished piece and feel… tired of having to decide what it wants from me, if that makes sense.

But losing interest? I don’t think so. I was mixing this blue-gray yesterday, actually, the color of the sky right before it rains, and then I remembered this wall in my grandmother’s kitchen that had almost the same shade—anyway, no, I don’t think I’ve stopped enjoying things. I’m just a bit tangled up in everything right now.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down, hopeless, or lost pleasure or interest in most things for several days in a row?

I don’t think so… not for several days in a row like that. I mean, I have low moments, usually when I see the list of everything I haven’t finished, and then I’ll end up staring at the paintbrushes instead of actually using them.

But it’s not like everything feels empty or hopeless. I still get pulled into things—colors, textures, silly little ideas. Yesterday I spent way too long looking at the way dust collected on a windowsill because it looked like a tiny landscape, which is probably not helpful for my deadlines, but… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve lost pleasure in most things.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or lacking energy most days, even when you haven’t been doing much?

I’m not sure I’d say unusually tired. I mean, I do get worn out, but sometimes that’s after I’ve spent the whole morning moving canvases around because I suddenly decide the light is wrong in the corner by the window.

When I haven’t done much… I don’t know. I haven’t really been tracking it that way. Some days I feel sort of scattered more than tired, like I’m using energy in little useless sparks instead of one good flame. But lacking energy most days? I don’t think I can honestly say I’ve noticed that.
Have you noticed yourself feeling restless, like you can’t sit still or slow your mind down, especially when you're thinking about everything you have to do?

Yes, that sounds… closer. Like yesterday, from the morning on, I had this sort of humming current under my skin. Not exactly nervous, just—unable to land anywhere.

I kept rearranging the studio, then I started drafting proposals, then I was emailing people about things that probably could’ve waited, and then I got very involved in sorting brushes by size, which reminded me of this old supply shop I used to go to that smelled like dust and linseed oil—anyway. Sitting quietly felt almost impossible. My mind kept jumping to the next thing I should be doing.
Do you often find it hard to focus on tasks, even when you want to, or do you get easily distracted by things around you or by your own thoughts?

Yes—yes, I do. I’ll sit down meaning to finish a plate for a contract, and I really do want to finish it, but then a bird lands at the window and suddenly I’m watching the shape of its feet, or I notice the hardware catalog on the table and think maybe those hinges could be used for something sculptural.

And then that turns into an idea for a workshop, half-formed, not even practical yet, and before I know it the plate is just sitting there untouched. It’s frustrating because it isn’t that I don’t care about the task. I just get pulled off course so easily.
Have you found yourself jumping into activities or making decisions without thinking them through, like taking on too many projects or spending money you can't really afford to spend?

Yes… I suppose I have. I mean, at the time it felt very sensible, almost necessary. I bought this large-format printer, and the specialty papers to go with it, and then lighting, because the light in the cottage-studio is never quite right—well, it’s beautiful in the late afternoon, but terrible for photographing work.

And then there were renovation materials, just a few things at first, except “a few things” became more than that. I kept thinking the money would sort itself out once the big breakthrough happened, like the work would pay for everything because of course it would.

Only later did I look at it properly and realize I’d put the cottage-studio much closer to trouble than I meant to. That was… frightening, actually.
Have you had periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or your thoughts were racing faster than usual, even if it felt good or productive at the time?

Yes, the energetic part, definitely. It wasn’t like I woke up and calmly decided to be productive, it was more like there was this humming current in me from the morning onward. I couldn’t quite settle.

I kept moving around the studio—rearranging things, then starting proposals, then sending emails, then fussing with supplies and brushes and all of that. And then I’d notice something small, like the way the paper was stacked, and that would become a whole other task. Sitting still felt almost impossible, even though part of me knew I was just… ricocheting from one thing to the next.

Have you had a period of time—lasting at least a few days—where your mood was unusually high, overly confident, or irritable, not just feeling good because something went well but in a way that felt different from your usual self?

Yes… yes, that sounds familiar. There were days—several in a row, I think—where I felt almost lit from the inside, like everything in the studio and the garden had finally started to make sense together. I’d walk out and see the beds and the tools and the worktables and think, “Of course, this is all coming together.”

But if someone interrupted that, or asked something practical—like about invoices, or whether a plan was actually affordable—I could get very sharp. Sharper than I meant to be. It wasn’t just being pleased because something went well. It felt… bigger than that, and a bit unlike me, though at the time I didn’t really want anyone pointing that out.

Have you had a period of time—lasting at least a week—where your mood was abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable, not just feeling good because something went well but in a way that was clearly different from your usual self?

Yes, I think it did go on about that long… most days, anyway. I felt unusually buoyant, almost lit up, like the studio and the garden were finally clicking into place with each other.

It sounds nice when I say it that way, and parts of it were nice—the light on the beds in the morning, the way the worktables looked when I’d moved them—but it wasn’t just ordinary happiness. If someone asked about invoices or questioned whether my plans made sense, I could snap at them terribly sharply. Much more sharply than I’d usually mean to.

You mentioned feeling unusually buoyant for about a week. Was there a specific time during that week when your mood was so high or irritable that others might have noticed it was different from your usual self?

Yes, I think so. There were a few points that week where it must have been obvious. I felt so buoyant and lit up, like the studio and the garden were finally—oh, I don’t know, speaking the same language. I kept seeing connections everywhere, which sounds a bit dramatic, but it felt very clear at the time.

And then if someone asked something ordinary, like about invoices, or whether one of my plans actually made sense, I could snap. Not just answer firmly—snap. I remember getting sharp over practical questions that probably weren’t meant as criticism at all. So yes, I think other people would have noticed I wasn’t quite my usual self.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the unusually high or irritable mood during that week was noticeable and different from usual, which directly matches elevated or irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. There were a few points that week where it must have been obvious. I felt so buoyant and lit up, like the studio and the garden were finally—oh, I don’t know, speaking the same language. I kept seeing connections everywhere, which sounds a bit dramatic, but it felt very clear at the time.

And then if someone asked something ordinary, like about invoices, or whether one of my plans actually made sense, I could snap. Not just answer firmly—snap. I remember getting sharp over practical questions that probably weren’t meant as criticism at all. So yes, I think other people would have noticed I wasn’t quite my usual self.

inference.note: The patient has met criteria for a manic episode (F31.81) based on the presence of a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting at least one week, with increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep (inferred), distractibility, and involvement in multiple projects/activities. The absence of predominant depressive symptoms rules out bipolar II (F31.89) and supports the diagnosis of bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, mild.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's reason for seeking help.
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits clear symptoms of a manic episode, including elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, distractibility, and psychomotor agitation. These symptoms persisted for at least a week and caused noticeable change in functioning, meeting criteria for bipolar disorder, current episode manic, mild.
